analysis.one_liner: Bans rental application and tenant-screening fees, caps late fees, and requires upfront rent cost disclosure.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in June 2025 and referred to the Banking Committee, where no action has been taken and no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar owners of rental units that have federal backing or assistance — a wide swath of the rental market, including properties with FHA, VA, USDA, or Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac mortgages — from charging application fees or tenant screening and background check fees. It would cap late fees at under 3% of monthly rent and only allow them 15 days after rent is due. It would also require landlords to tell tenants before signing a lease what the total monthly cost is, plus any past litigation with tenants, ongoing pest or maintenance problems, and the rent increases over the past 10 years. Reporting an unpaid junk fee to a credit bureau would be treated as an illegal debt collection practice.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters in federally assisted or federally financed housing, who currently pay application and screening fees on top of rent and can be hit with surprise charges; applicants who often pay fees to multiple landlords just to be rejected; and tenants whose unpaid junk fees have damaged their credit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters facing application, screening, and late fees

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits owners of covered units from charging any fee in connection with a rental application [S2].
Prohibits charging tenants for criminal history, tenant screening, consumer report, or other background checks [S2].
Caps late fees below 3% of monthly rent and allows them only 15 days after rent is due, with disclosure in the lease [S2].
Requires pre-lease disclosure of total monthly cost including fees, past litigation with tenants, ongoing pest and maintenance issues, and rent increases in each of the past 10 years [S2].
Requires regulators to define rental junk fees and makes reporting an unpaid junk fee to a consumer reporting agency a violation of the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act [S2].

Coverage reaches units with HUD assistance and units on properties with federally backed single-family or multifamily mortgages, including FHA, VA, USDA, and Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac loans, which spans a large share of the rental market [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Landlords of covered properties, who would lose application, screening, and late fee income and would need to absorb screening costs themselves and make new disclosures; tenant screening and background check companies, whose landlord-paid-per-check revenue would shrink; and, to the extent landlords offset lost fees, applicants could face somewhat higher advertised rents.

drawbacks.text: Coverage is limited to federally assisted or federally financed units, so renters in properties with no federal mortgage or assistance tie would not be protected [S2].
Landlords would bear the cost of screening checks themselves, which some could pass through in higher rent — a tradeoff of shifting costs from per-applicant fees to the landlord [S2].
The bill relies on rulemaking by CFPB and the FTC within 180 days to define junk fees, leaving key terms to regulators rather than the statute itself [S2].
Banning application fees entirely removes a filter some small landlords use to deter frivolous applications, which could increase their screening workload [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For renters, the direct gains are concrete and immediate: no more paying $50-$100 in application and screening fees to multiple landlords for the privilege of being rejected, no surprise charges tacked onto rent, and knowing the full monthly cost and a building's problems before signing. The main cost-shifting risk is that landlords may raise advertised rents slightly to cover screening costs they now pay directly, but renters would see the true all-in price upfront and could comparison shop. The coverage gap — units with no federal tie — is the biggest design weakness.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, which has not taken it up; the Congress is still in session, so it simply sits waiting.

narrative.text: Sen. Merkley introduced the bill on June 24, 2025, joined by Sen. Sanders; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee [S1][S4].
It has one cosponsor, an Independent senator, and no further committee or floor action has been recorded [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Renters have gained nothing yet, and landlords of federally backed properties keep charging application, screening, and late fees while the bill sits untouched in committee.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Junk Fees for Renters Act and referred it to the Banking Committee

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction, named in the introduction as a co-sponsor

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action since — no markup, hearing on the bill, or vote has been recorded

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; support on the record so far is one Democrat and two Independents, and no Republican has cosponsored or publicly opposed the bill in the record.

industries.industry: Landlords of federally assisted or federally financed rental properties
industries.note: The bill eliminates application and screening fee income, caps late fees, and requires upfront disclosures for properties with HUD assistance or FHA, VA, USDA, or Fannie/Freddie mortgages. Landlords' interest in keeping these fees runs against renters who pay them.

industries.industry: Tenant screening and background check companies
industries.note: Screening firms sell background and consumer reports to landlords per applicant; banning tenant-paid screening fees removes that revenue stream from renters and reduces demand at the margin. Junk fees reported to credit bureaus would become an illegal collection practice.

They would lose disputed junk-fee tradelines that inflate reported debts, but remain the underlying channel for credit data; the bill regulates how junk fees reach them rather than their core business.

analysis.trajectory: With a Democratic-only sponsorship in a Republican-run Senate and a Banking Committee chair who controls the markup calendar, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or vote this Congress. Its realistic path is dying quietly in committee, or having its ideas picked up later in a larger housing package or by regulators (the FTC and CFPB have separately pursued junk fee rules) rather than through this bill itself.
